clinicalPearls: Retrosternal burning discomfort despite normal oesophageal acid exposure and no correlation between symptoms and reflux events
There is no evidence of erosive disease, eosinophilic oesophagitis or a major motility disorder
It characteristically responds poorly to acid-suppressing therapy, which helps distinguish it from reflux disease
It reflects oesophageal hypersensitivity and altered central pain processing rather than acid injury
Diagnosis requires endoscopy and ambulatory reflux monitoring showing physiological acid exposure with a negative symptom association
Management uses neuromodulators and psychological therapies rather than escalating acid suppression
reference.pathophysiology: Functional heartburn is a disorder of gut-brain interaction in which the sensation of heartburn occurs without pathological acid reflux. Oesophageal hypersensitivity, peripheral and central sensitisation of visceral pain pathways, and psychological factors generate the perception of burning despite normal acid exposure and no temporal link to reflux episodes. Because acid is not driving the symptom, acid suppression is largely ineffective, and treatment targets pain perception instead.
additionalInvestigations: Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy, typically normal, with biopsies to exclude eosinophilic oesophagitis
Ambulatory pH-impedance monitoring showing normal acid exposure and negative symptom association
Oesophageal manometry to exclude a major motility disorder
Review of prior response to acid suppression
redFlags: Dysphagia, weight loss or bleeding suggesting organic disease
Failure to fit the criteria on objective testing
reference.prognosis: The condition is benign but can be persistent and frustrating; symptoms often improve with neuromodulator therapy and psychological approaches once acid-related disease is excluded.
pitfalls: Escalating acid suppression that will not help
Not performing objective reflux testing before diagnosis
Overlooking cardiac causes of chest discomfort
references: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
management: Explain that acid is not driving the symptom and that escalating acid suppression is unlikely to help
Neuromodulators such as tricyclic antidepressants to reduce oesophageal hypersensitivity as the mainstay of treatment
Psychological therapies such as cognitive behavioural therapy, hypnotherapy or relaxation techniques
Withdraw ineffective proton pump inhibitor therapy once reflux disease has been excluded
